expurgate

EK-spur-gayt · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To expurgate is to remove offensive or objectionable material from something.

The museum agreed to expurgate the exhibit label after several visitors complained about its language.

Example

Early American editions of the play were often expurgated before being taught in schools.

Editors weren't just editing for length -- they were specifically cutting the parts they considered offensive, which is exactly expurgate.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

censor: To censor is to cut or silence material an authority disapproves of — political, military, or moral — anything from one word to a whole broadcast. To expurgate is the narrower editorial act: removing offensive passages from a text or recording so a cleaned-up version can be released. Censors wield official power; expurgating prepares an edition.

bowdlerize: To bowdlerize is to scrub a work of so much supposedly improper material that the result is weakened or ridiculous — the word mocks Thomas Bowdler's rewritten family-friendly Shakespeare. To expurgate is the neutral term: removing genuinely offensive material, with no suggestion of going too far. Every bowdlerized text has been expurgated, but clumsily and to excess.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

preserve: to keep something whole and unchanged, removing nothing

Where it sits · how far the cutting of content goes

edit → expurgate → suppress

edit vs. expurgate: Editing simply revises a text for clarity or length; expurgating it specifically removes offensive content.

suppress vs. expurgate: Expurgating removes specific offensive passages from a work; suppressing blocks the entire work from being seen at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ex-: out (Latin)

root — purg: to cleanse (Latin (purgare))

suffix — -ate: to make or perform an action (Latin)

Put it together: Expurgate comes from Latin ex- ('out') + purgare ('to cleanse') + -ate -- literally 'to cleanse out.'

Use the root in a new word: purge: Once a year, the library purges its oldest magazine bins.
